prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single-part prize. The case is a quantitative prediction (the 2011 continuum model of Bistritzer and MacDonald) followed by a discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) that has been reproduced by many independent laboratories and has produced a tunable platform now extended to other moire systems. The citation I propose rests only on what is established: flat bands, correlated insulating states and the existence of superconductivity, with no claim to have explained the pairing mechanism. On that wording the unsettled mechanism is a question for the next decade, not a flaw in the discovery. The round-1 discussion did not weaken the scientific case; it sharpened the comparison with optical lattice clocks (B002), which wins on maturity and compact credit but, in my judgement, adds less new physics than a new regime of strongly correlated matter.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my own position is maturity and attribution, and the exchange has made it heavier, not lighter. The field is about eight years old, the pairing mechanism is open, and the experimental credit is truncated: Cao and other early authors sit outside the three-name limit, and I cannot call that cost small. Five colleagues put B002 first, with a clean two-name credit, independent reproduction in several national laboratories and 10^-18 performance. If the committee decides that a settled result must come first, B002 is a defensible choice and I would not regard it as an error. I also see no workable two-part prize with B002: it would need five names, and cutting to three unique people would damage both parts.

responses.point: Kroll holds B002 first on a single original idea (the magic-wavelength lattice), a 10^-18 realisation, reproduction in many laboratories and a compact Katori-Ye credit, and reads the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a foundation more than as an overlap.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and attribution points without reservation, and I agree the reproduction record is exactly what B038 still lacks in some respects. Where I stay apart is the novelty reading. The 2005 comb and 2012 single-system prizes honour the tools that make a lattice clock possible, and a reader can still see the clock as the best application of a prized line, even if the magic-wavelength idea is original. The graphene work opens a regime that did not exist as an experimental object before 2018. I would say this is a difference in weighting, not a dispute over facts. Your disclosure of a Boulder research stay seems to me a perceived link to be recorded, not a reason to discount your scientific argument.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B038 for the theory-plus-experiment structure and says he could accept B002 as the second part of a two-part prize, while flagging the timing risk and thematic crowding with the 2010 and 2016 condensed-matter prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the structure, and I take your crowding point as a real cost. I think the 2010 prize (graphene as a material) and the 2016 prize (topological phases) are distinct from correlated physics in flat bands, but I accept a committee could weigh that differently. On the two-part idea I looked at the arithmetic: B038 (three names) plus B002 (two names) gives five people, and the three-person limit across the whole configuration forces an unacceptable cut. Dropping Bistritzer would break the prediction half of the case, and dropping Ye or Katori would break the clock. So I do not propose it and I would ask you whether you see a fair way to do it that I have missed. We also agree that the citation must avoid any claim about the pairing mechanism.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B002 first, arguing that a Katori-Ye two-laureate prize needs no one essential to be left out, that the performance is independently verified, and that waiting for the redefinition of the second is not decisive.
responses.response: I agree that the timing argument about the redefinition is not decisive, and I would not ask the committee to wait for it. Your question to Eriksson and me asks what would make B038 mature enough. For me, three things would help: independent confirmation of superconductivity across device types, a settled account of the flat-band-versus-strong-coupling regime of the correlated insulators, and a clearer public record on who made the 2018 devices work. None of these is a condition I would put on the award as such, but if none were met in a few years, I would move to B002. The remaining difference is that I place the open question about the pairing mechanism behind the scientific content, not in front of it.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the Higgs discovery (B053) first on certainty and consequence, names attribution under the three-person limit as the decisive weakness, and lists B002 and B038 as the better-attributed alternatives.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is scientifically exceptional and mature, and your honesty about attribution is useful. I do not see a principled rule for three names against two collaborations of thousands: founding-era leadership, discovery-year spokespersons and analysis conveners each produce a different, defensible trio. A prize whose names must be chosen by an arbitrary rule is, in my judgement, less sound than one where the credit follows from the discovery itself. I therefore leave B053 outside my configuration and alternatives, though I would not dispute your account of its scientific weight.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges a field of about eight years, with an open pairing mechanism, to be mature enough; I cannot give a decisive argument either way.
Whether the experimental credit can fairly be limited to Jarillo-Herrero when Cao and other early authors did much of the 2018 work, and whether earlier moire experiments are fairly omitted.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make lattice clocks cumulative, which is the point on which my preference over B002 turns.
Whether my disciplinary taste for minimal models that organise complex phenomenology is shifting my weighting of conceptual novelty against maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No documented conflict with any credited candidate. KPZ (B056), my alternative, touches stochastic-growth and random-matrix topics adjacent to my own research, but I have no documented collaboration with Takeuchi, Kardar or Zhang. I have none with the B038 or B002 names either, and I do not need to recuse on any shortlisted part.
